doc.title: Warren Smith interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, March 17, 2018

title: Knowing when to end, exaggeration, and composing for percussion
summary: Judgment from decades of performing; exaggerating volume; assigning sounds to instruments; the Partch bass marimba again.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: I was going to ask you, in some cases, how do you know when to end a piece of music that is basically being spontaneously created.

You have to develop a judgement for that. You have to develop that judgement over a period of time. And I feel now at this stage in my life, you know, after like 56 years of presentation, that I can tell when an audience might be bored. I can see restlessness, I can see people moving instead of everybody like this. And you get to the point where you can actually from the stage almost orchestrate the audience reaction you know. And if you have that big of an insight, and experience gives you that.
Good answer. You said this thing I saw, that you like exaggeration.
Can you give me a couple examples?

Yes, in particular volume. You know volume can go both ways. You can, you know, exaggerate emotion and play a very quiet sound you know. Or you can start something very soft and let it expand itself so it comes up. Now these are shapes you understand. But I think it’s more akin to like a visual artist. You know because you can paint these pictures in the air and the audience looks at them and responds in the fashion that eventually you can almost anticipate what the audience is going to do. Or you can say I won’t do that ‘cause I don’t think that’s going to be responded to well. So that might be my only restriction at this point.

I see. Wow. You’ve got a lot of food for thought here. How do you, you mentioned before that out of the blue you might start doing some physical motion and you’ve got to write that down. Now that could be a kernel for a composition —
And then do you assign like an instrument or something in your head to that — maybe the marimba should be doing this, and you start orchestrating it?

It depends on my interpretation of the quality of the sound that I want to reproduce or that I want to hear reproduced. There are certain fat sounds like from a bass violin that you don’t get from anything else. And percussion in particular has these qualities. You know a bass drum is the lowest sound in the orchestra. And you can hit it very softly or you can marry it with a high sound, like a cymbal or a flute or something very high pitched and get that bass, and it gives it a body that it doesn’t have. It like allows one sound to ride on the other. And everybody feels that. I was just talking to somebody, I mentioned Harry Partch before. He had an instrument called the bass marimba. And it had only four keys on it. And the mallet was the handle was like the lower end of a baseball bat and the head was like a soft, sixteen inch softball. And you hit this instrument, this particular bar, and you could see these sixteen vibrations. Physically you could see them. But you couldn’t hear it. But you could feel all sixteen vibrations in your stomach you know. And when you get sensitive to things like that, the certain sounds that are above your hearing capacity, but you feel something, you can maybe feel it in your teeth, you can feel it in. We all experience this in some way, you know a car screeches and there is an anticipation — what’s going to happen, is there going to be a bang? All these things are like we’re conditioned to this. So I try to take advantage of previous conditioning and try to manipulate that so it stimulates the reaction that I want from an audience.
